title: The Night Tuskegee's Third Brick Kiln Fell
conflicts: Washington's own two accounts differ: Up from Slavery (1901) has three failed kilns, a watch pawned for $15 and a successful fourth attempt; his 1899 account quoted by M. B. Thrasher (Popular Science Monthly) says they could not burn bricks at all and the pawned gold watch paid a skilled man to burn them and teach the students. Story gives both. Output: 1,200,000 bricks 'last season' (Up from Slavery) vs 1,500,000 'last year alone' (The Story of My Life and Work, 1900); story says 'more than a million a year, by Washington's counts'. Farm loan figures differ ($250, $200 down, $500) and are not used.
notes: Funding changed from the slate's 'nonprofit' to 'mixed' (state salary appropriation plus Northern donations and student labour). Washington gives no year; the story uses dated markers from The Story of My Life and Work (April 1883 plan to build with farm clay; spring 1884 'two kilns of bricks' made). Up from Slavery is used only as a story source, not for the quote.
